title: Back Attack Basics
description: Snapdowns, go-behinds, turtle-top back takes, and rear naked strangle mechanics for building a basic back-attack pathway.

media.title: Snap down for BJJ (Lachlan Giles)
notes: Context: Lachlan teaches the snapdown as a way to break posture and create go-behind/back-attack opportunities, especially by forcing posture instead of just yanking on the head.
- [00:24-01:51] Start from head/shoulder contact and use hand fighting, head position, and leg threat reactions to make the opponent bring their posture forward.
- [02:33-02:55] Useful snapdown grips include one hand behind the head and the other on the shoulder/triceps area.
- [04:23-05:38] Inside hand position matters so they cannot hang off your head or shoulders while you snap.
- [05:41-06:18] Do not go straight to the snap every time. Push, threaten the legs, or make them push back so the snap has a reaction to work with.
- [06:23-07:04] The movement comes heavily from the legs: step/retract the lead leg and drop weight so the hands guide the head rather than doing all the work.
- [07:00-08:55] After the snap, keep a chin strap, put your shoulder in front of their shoulder, and shake them down if needed.
- [10:54-12:31] To go behind, block the near arm, step the knee outside, and spin to a seatbelt/back position.

media.title: #1 Takedown In Wrestling With David Taylor
notes: Context: David Taylor presents the go-behind as the highest-percentage wrestling score from front headlock/front head trap situations.
- [00:00-01:05] Treat front headlock as a scoring position, not a stalemate.
- [01:08-01:27] First priority: put their head to their hand to create the angle.
- [01:27-01:43] Second priority: block or drag the arm so they cannot square back up while you circle.
- [01:43-02:44] Keep your chest high on their back; if your chest comes off, they can circle and force a neutral/no-score position.
- [03:01-03:19] Circle to the corner, finish to the hip, and keep moving through the score.
- [03:24-03:58] Be decisive about which side you go behind on.

media.title: The best way to take the back from turtle #bjj #jiujitsu
notes: Context: this short teaches the two-on-one leg method for taking the back from top turtle.
- [00:00-00:18] Drive in and secure a two-on-one grip on the leg.
- [00:18-00:28] Push their knee down to the mat so it becomes easy to insert the first hook.
- [00:32-00:46] If they put the shoulder to the ground and their hips leave the space between your knees, accelerate with your knee so you roll through.
- [00:46-00:58] Treat this as a simple recurring sequence to drill: two-on-one leg control, knee down, first hook, roll-through follow if their shoulder drops.

media.title: Back Attack Secrets with Gordon Ryan
notes: Context: Gordon shows a straightjacket-style hand-trapping path from back control, especially from the underhook side where hand trapping is easier but feeding the strangle is harder.
- [00:27-01:20] On the underhook side, go ear-to-ear to close the space their head and shoulders would escape into.
- [01:21-01:53] Strip the primary defensive hand, then switch to cross-wrist control when the secondary hand comes up to pull your choking hand down.
- [01:54-02:18] Split the hands and glue them to the opponent's torso so the one-on-one grips are reinforced by their body instead of floating in space.
- [02:19-02:49] Use the leg to trap the wrist, cross the ankles, then return to one-on-one control to create a one-attacking-hand-versus-zero-defensive-hands scenario.
- [02:51-03:40] To feed the strangle from the underhook side, bring your shoulder line toward your elbow, then use gravity to feed the hand behind the head.
- [04:32-05:17] Do not pull your elbow backward and lose ear-to-ear control while feeding the strangle.

media.title: The One Submission Every Grappler Must Know - Gordon Ryan
notes: Context: Gordon focuses on finishing mechanics for the rear naked strangle once the choking hand is already in position.
- [00:22-00:38] The main problem is not just squeezing harder; poor hand setting can make you burn out with a locked-looking strangle.
- [00:43-01:20] Concave the shoulders and hollow the body to create space for the support arm to shoot through.
- [01:47-02:00] Get the back of the support hand to the partner's head and connect fingertips to bicep before finishing.
- [02:02-02:14] Before squeezing, bring both elbows together to strengthen the fingertip-to-bicep connection.
- [02:16-02:45] The goal is a stable figure-four connection that holds even when the opponent pushes the elbow or starts common escape reactions.
